content: Machine learning is a branch of AI where computers learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed. It involves training algorithms on datasets so they can make predictions or decisions on new, unseen data.

Supervised learning uses labeled data to train models. You give the algorithm input-output pairs and it learns the mapping. Common examples include classification (spam detection) and regression (house price prediction).
Unsupervised learning finds hidden patterns in data without labels. Clustering and dimensionality reduction are the main types. K-means clustering and PCA are popular algorithms in this category.

Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers to learn complex patterns. It powers things like image recognition, speech processing, and language models. It needs a lot of data and compute to work well.

Neural networks are inspired by the human brain. They have layers of interconnected nodes that process information. Each connection has a weight that gets adjusted during training through backpropagation.

NLP deals with how computers understand and generate human language. It covers tasks like sentiment analysis, translation, text generation, and question answering. Modern NLP is dominated by transformer models.

Transformers are the architecture behind most modern language models. Introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need', they use self-attention mechanisms to process sequences in parallel rather than sequentially.

LLMs like GPT-4 and Claude are massive neural networks trained on huge text datasets. They can generate text, answer questions, write code, and more. They work by predicting the next token in a sequence.

Fine-tuning takes a pre-trained model and adapts it to a specific task using a smaller, specialized dataset. It's much cheaper than training from scratch and can dramatically improve performance on domain-specific tasks.

Prompt engineering is the practice of designing effective inputs to get better outputs from language models. Techniques include few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, and providing clear context and constraints.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with text generation. Instead of relying only on trained knowledge, the model retrieves relevant documents and uses them to generate more accurate, grounded answers.

Vector databases store data as high-dimensional vectors (embeddings) and enable fast similarity search. ChromaDB, Pinecone, and Weaviate are popular options. They are essential for building semantic search and RAG systems.

Embeddings are numerical representations of data (text, images, etc.) in a continuous vector space. Similar items end up close together in this space. They enable semantic search because you can find related content by measuring vector distance.

Deploying an ML model means making it available for real-world use. This involves packaging the model, setting up serving infrastructure, creating APIs, and monitoring performance. Tools like FastAPI, Docker, and cloud services are commonly used.

MLOps combines ML with DevOps practices. It covers the full lifecycle: data management, model training, deployment, monitoring, and retraining. The goal is to make ML systems reliable, reproducible, and maintainable in production.

When building AI-powered APIs, consider latency, rate limiting, error handling, and response format. Streaming responses can improve user experience for LLM applications. Always validate inputs and handle edge cases.

AI ethics covers fairness, accountability, transparency, and privacy. Models can inherit biases from training data, and it is important to test for and mitigate these biases before deploying AI systems in the real world.

Common metrics include accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score for classification. For language models, we use perplexity, BLEU, ROUGE, and human evaluation. Choosing the right metric depends on what matters most for your use case.

Overfitting happens when a model memorizes training data instead of learning general patterns. Signs include high training accuracy but poor test performance. Solutions include regularization, dropout, early stopping, and getting more data.

Transfer learning reuses knowledge from a model trained on one task to help with a different but related task. It is why pre-trained models like BERT and GPT are so powerful - they already understand language structure.

Gradient descent is the main optimization algorithm used to train neural networks. It iteratively adjusts model weights in the direction that reduces the loss function. Variants include SGD, Adam, and AdaGrad.

Data preprocessing involves cleaning, normalizing, and transforming raw data before feeding it to a model. This includes handling missing values, encoding categorical variables, scaling features, and splitting into train/test sets.

RL trains agents to make decisions by rewarding good actions and penalizing bad ones. It is used in game-playing AI, robotics, and recommendation systems. RLHF (RL from Human Feedback) is used to align language models.

Computer vision enables machines to interpret visual information from images and videos. CNNs (Convolutional Neural Networks) are the backbone architecture. Applications include object detection, face recognition, and autonomous driving.

Companies are increasingly adopting AI for customer service, process automation, predictive analytics, and product recommendations. The key challenge is not the technology itself but integrating AI into existing workflows and measuring ROI.

Structured outputs force language models to return data in a specific format like JSON or Pydantic objects. This makes it much easier to use LLM responses in applications since you get predictable, parseable data.

AI agents are systems that can plan, use tools, and take actions to accomplish goals. They combine LLMs with tool use, memory, and reasoning capabilities. Frameworks like LangGraph and AutoGen help build agent systems.

Semantic search finds results based on meaning rather than exact keyword matching. It uses embeddings to represent queries and documents as vectors, then finds the closest matches. This is much better than traditional search for natural language queries.

Tokenization breaks text into smaller units (tokens) that models can process. BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) and WordPiece are common methods. Understanding tokenization helps you estimate costs and manage context window limits.

The context window is the maximum amount of text a language model can process at once. GPT-4 supports up to 128K tokens. Managing context efficiently is crucial for applications dealing with long documents or conversations.

LLM hallucination is when models generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information. RAG, grounding, and careful prompt design can reduce hallucinations. Always verify critical outputs from language models.
